narrationScript: The ARM architecture has a rich history of continuous innovation. It began with ARMv1 in 1985, an early 32-bit RISC processor. By ARMv4 in 1994, important additions like halfword and signed byte loads, and the Thumb 16-bit compressed instruction set, significantly improved code density. ARMv5, introduced in 1999, brought DSP instructions and Jazelle Java acceleration, expanding its application space. A major leap came with ARMv6 in 2001, which added SIMD instructions, the flexible Thumb-2 instruction set mixing 16 and 32-bit instructions, and crucial multiprocessing support. This led to the widely used ARM11 series. ARMv7, from 2005, defined three profiles: Application, Real-time, and Microcontroller, and introduced powerful NEON 128-bit SIMD and VFPv3 floating-point. This generation powered the popular Cortex-A series. The true revolution arrived with ARMv8-A in 2011, ushering in the 64-bit era with AArch64, while maintaining AArch32 for backward compatibility. This version laid the groundwork for today's high-performance processors like Apple Silicon. Most recently, ARMv9-A in 2021 further advanced the architecture with SVE2, Confidential Compute Architecture, and Memory Tagging Extension for enhanced security.
